reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: A rare inherited channelopathy defined by an abnormally short QT interval and predisposition to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias
May present with palpitations, atrial fibrillation at a young age, syncope, or sudden cardiac death, and can occur across all ages including infancy
The ECG shows a persistently short QT interval with tall, peaked, and symmetrical T waves
The short QT interval does not lengthen appropriately with slowing heart rate, unlike normal physiology
Diagnosis combines the ECG measurement with symptoms, family history, and genetic findings
Caused by gain-of-function mutations in cardiac potassium channels or loss-of-function in calcium channels that shorten repolarisation
An implantable defibrillator is the main protection against sudden death in high-risk patients, with quinidine considered to prolong repolarisation
A short refractory period predisposes to both atrial fibrillation and ventricular fibrillation
reference.pathophysiology: Short QT syndrome arises from ion channel abnormalities that accelerate cardiac repolarisation, most often gain-of-function mutations enhancing outward potassium currents or loss-of-function affecting inward calcium current. Shortened action potential duration and refractory periods reduce the wavelength of electrical activation, creating a substrate for re-entry in both atria and ventricles. This electrical heterogeneity underlies the propensity to atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation despite a structurally normal heart.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary QT shortening from hyperkalaemia, hypercalcaemia, or acidosis
Effects of digoxin or other drugs
Lone atrial fibrillation of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Serial 12-lead ECGs with careful QT interval measurement corrected for rate
Exclusion of electrolyte and metabolic causes of a short QT
Ambulatory monitoring for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias
Echocardiography to confirm a structurally normal heart
Genetic testing of relevant potassium and calcium channel genes
redFlags: Aborted sudden cardiac death or documented ventricular fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation presenting at an unusually young age
Family history of sudden cardiac death
reference.prognosis: The syndrome carries a meaningful lifetime risk of sudden cardiac death, which can be the first event even in previously asymptomatic individuals. Defibrillator therapy protects high-risk patients, and pharmacological repolarisation-prolonging treatment may reduce arrhythmic events; prognosis depends heavily on prior arrhythmic history and appropriate risk stratification.
pitfalls: Overlooking a short QT interval because attention focuses on long-QT abnormalities
Failing to exclude reversible metabolic causes before diagnosing the inherited syndrome
Underestimating sudden death risk in an asymptomatic person with a strong family history
Missing early-onset atrial fibrillation as a clue to the diagnosis
